varieties.name: Newtown Pippin
varieties.summary: Very firm, crisp flesh that is sharp at picking and needs months in store; it then becomes rich and aromatic with a tangy sweetness and the pineapple-like note it is famous for. Excellent for juice and pies.

varieties.name: Nonpareil
varieties.summary: Tender, fine-grained greenish flesh with a lively, wine-like acidity and a rich aromatic depth that softens and sweetens through the winter. Best treated as a mid-winter apple rather than eaten from the tree.

varieties.name: Norfolk Beauty
varieties.summary: Rather soft, loose, somewhat dry flesh with a clean acidity. It cooks quickly to a creamy froth that needs little sugar and has a light lemony note.

varieties.name: Norfolk Beefing
varieties.summary: Very firm, coarse, juicy flesh that is strongly acidic at picking. It sweetens slowly in store and by late winter or spring can be eaten fresh; baked or dried it becomes dense, rich and sweet.

varieties.name: Norfolk Royal Russet
varieties.summary: Rich, sweet and nutty with a pear-like russet character and enough acidity to stay lively. The flesh is firm and juicy, less dry and spongy than Egremont Russet. Many tasters rank it among the best-flavoured English apples.

varieties.name: Norland
varieties.summary: A sweet, juicy summer apple with a light McIntosh-like flavour from its Melba side. Crisp at first but softens within weeks, and the white flesh browns quickly once cut.

varieties.name: Northern Spy
varieties.summary: Crisp, very juicy, fine-grained flesh with a brisk, aromatic sweet-tart flavour that holds up well in store. It keeps its shape and tang when baked, which is why it is a favourite pie apple in North America.

varieties.name: Nuvar Cheerfull Gold
varieties.summary: A balanced sweet-sharp apple with a pleasant tang. It lacks the layered aromatics of Cox but has crisper flesh, closer to Golden Delicious, and keeps well.

varieties.name: Nuvar Golden Hills
varieties.summary: Crisp and juicy with a sweet, fairly rich flavour; a little sweeter than its Greensleeves parent.

varieties.name: Opal
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy and sweet with a tangy edge; the fine cream-yellow flesh has a quince-like fragrance with a hint of pear. It barely browns when cut thanks to low polyphenol oxidase.

varieties.name: Opalescent
varieties.summary: Firm, fairly crisp cream flesh with a sweet, gentle flavour and some balancing acidity; a few growers note delicate floral hints. Used for baking as well as eating.

varieties.name: Orin
varieties.summary: Very sweet, honeyed and juicy, with a distinctive perfume but very little acidity. Admirers love its fragrance; those who like a sharp apple may find it flat.

varieties.name: Orleans Reinette
varieties.summary: Firm, fine-textured flesh that is not especially juicy but carries a rich, sweet, nutty flavour with balancing acidity, very like Blenheim Orange. One of the best late apples for flavour rather than crunch.

varieties.name: Otava
varieties.summary: Usually described as a sweet, juicy yellow apple with mild acidity, keeping well into late winter. Independent tasting notes are limited.

varieties.name: Oxford Conquest
varieties.summary: The National Fruit Collection describes rather tough flesh with an acid flavour; little else is recorded, so it is best seen as a sharp, firm late apple.

varieties.name: Palmer's Rosey
varieties.summary: Crisp, fairly tender flesh with a noticeably aromatic flavour for an August apple.

varieties.name: Parkland
varieties.summary: Soft, sweet and juicy when ripe but rather tart and plain in flavour; best eaten straight off the tree or turned into sauce, since it keeps poorly.

varieties.name: Patte de Loup
varieties.summary: Fine, dense, firm flesh, not especially juicy, with a sweet, gently acid and perfumed flavour carrying a faint aniseed note, in the manner of the French fennel-scented russets. Develops in store through winter.

varieties.name: Peasgood's Nonsuch
varieties.summary: Tender, slightly coarse, moderately juicy flesh with a gentle sweet-sharp flavour that is pleasant raw. Its real strength is cooking: it breaks down into a sweet, smooth puree needing little sugar, ideal for baked apples and sauce.

varieties.name: Peck's Pleasant
varieties.summary: Crisp, tender yellowish flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and strongly aromatic flavour. Old American writers ranked it 'very good to best' for eating fresh through the winter.

varieties.name: Pig's Nose Pippin
varieties.summary: Fine-grained, crisp cream flesh with a sweet flavour. Few other tasting details are recorded.

varieties.name: Pilot
varieties.summary: Firm, juicy flesh with a sweet-sharp, fairly brisk flavour that becomes sweeter and more aromatic after a few months in store. A true winter keeper rather than an apple for picking and eating.

varieties.name: Pink Pearl
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy, bright pink flesh with a tart-sweet, sharp flavour that many liken to pink grapefruit; close to a cooking apple in acidity. Makes attractive pink sauce and juice.

varieties.name: Pinova
varieties.summary: Crisp and juicy with an intense, well-balanced sweet-sharp flavour that shows its Cox ancestry; neither cloying nor tart, and it keeps its quality in store.

varieties.name: Pitmaston Pine Apple
varieties.summary: Firm, juicy yellow flesh that is very sweet and rich, with honey and nutty notes and a hint of pineapple balanced by some acidity. A small apple with a remarkably intense flavour.

varieties.name: Pixie
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy cream flesh with an intense, Cox-style aromatic flavour, sharper and more refreshing than Cox when first picked and mellowing in store.

varieties.name: Polka
varieties.summary: Sweet, crisp and juicy with a mild, McIntosh-family character that some compare to Spartan. A pleasant eater rather than a complex one; it does not keep long.

varieties.name: Polly
varieties.summary: Soft white flesh with a sweet, gently acidic flavour; usable both raw and in the kitchen.

varieties.name: Polly Prosser
varieties.summary: Firm, rather coarse yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and rich flavour. Few further tasting notes are published.

varieties.name: Pomme Gris
varieties.summary: A rich, sweet, nutty russet with firm, fine flesh and a sprightly finish; improves for a few weeks after picking.

varieties.name: Prairie Spy
varieties.summary: Firm, dense, crisp flesh with a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavour that improves after some weeks in store. Excellent for baking and pies, and one of the longest keepers among hardy apples.

varieties.name: Primrose Pippin
varieties.summary: A modern-style crisp, juicy apple with more sugar (about 18% by refractometer), acidity and fruitiness than most late-season supermarket types. The raiser and the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan both describe the balance as excellent.

varieties.name: Priscilla
varieties.summary: Crisp, fairly juicy flesh with a sweet, moderately tart flavour; descriptions vary from mild and Delicious-like to pleasantly sharp. Eats well fresh and also cooks acceptably.

varieties.name: Pristine
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy yellowish flesh with a tart-sweet flavour that is unusually good for such an early apple; the sharpness softens as the fruit fully ripens. Also good for sauce.

varieties.name: Queen Cox
varieties.summary: Like Cox, with firm, juicy, slightly acid flesh and a rich, aromatic flavour that brings floral, pear-drop and honeyed notes into balance. It improves for a few weeks after picking.

varieties.name: Rajka
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy, cream-yellow flesh with a sweet flavour balanced by fair acidity, often compared with Elstar. Pleasant and aromatic rather than complex; it sweetens further after a few weeks in store.

varieties.name: Rave
varieties.summary: Very crisp, shattering, juice-laden flesh in the Honeycrisp mould, with a brighter tart edge than its parent balanced by good sugar. An eating apple only: the flesh collapses when cooked.

varieties.name: Red Astrachan
varieties.summary: Juicy, crisp white flesh, often tinged red, with a brisk tart flavour and some aroma. Good eaten straight from the tree but goes mealy within days; best known as a sauce and pie apple.

varieties.name: Red Delicious
varieties.summary: Very sweet, juicy flesh with little acidity and only a light aroma, under a thick, tough skin. Freshly picked fruit from a warm climate is pleasant, but stored supermarket fruit is often mealy and bland.

varieties.name: Red Falstaff
varieties.summary: Crisp and very juicy, with a sweet-sharp balance that combines the zest of James Grieve with Golden Delicious sweetness. Good fresh or pressed for juice.

varieties.name: Red James Grieve
varieties.summary: As James Grieve: very juicy, soft-textured flesh with a lively, refreshing acidity when first picked that mellows to a sweeter balance after a week or two.

varieties.name: Red Sauce
varieties.summary: Coarse, rather dry flesh with a mild, lightly acid flavour; more interesting for its pink colour than its eating quality. Cooks to a rosy sauce.

varieties.name: Red Sentinel
varieties.summary: Sharp and not for eating raw; it can be used for jelly, but it is grown mainly for its long winter fruit display and as food for birds.

varieties.name: Red Windsor
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy, yellowish flesh with an aromatic Cox-like flavour that is a touch sharper and fresher than Cox, and a honeyed sweetness when fully ripe. Picked early it is noticeably tart.

varieties.name: Redfree
varieties.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a fresh, mildly sweet-sharp balance; some tasters note an unusual character attributed to its crab-apple ancestry. Holds quality for a few weeks in the fridge and dries well.
